q: What is the Software Carbon Intensity (SCI) score and how do I calculate it?
title: Software Carbon Intensity (SCI) explained
short: The SCI score is a rate: the carbon emitted per unit of work your software does, such as per API call or per active user. ISO/IEC 21031:2024 sets the formula: energy used times grid carbon intensity, plus a share of the hardware's embodied emissions, divided by your chosen functional unit.

p: SCI = ((E x I) + M) per R.
ul: E: energy the software used over the period, in kWh, for the servers, storage and network you include.
I: carbon intensity of that electricity, in grams per kWh, for the grid region where it ran.
M: embodied emissions of the hardware, shared out by time and by the part of the machine you reserved.
R: the functional unit, the thing you divide by, such as one API call, one user, one transaction or one GB processed.

sections.h: How to share out embodied emissions
p: M = total embodied emissions of the device x (hours you reserved it / expected life in hours) x (resources you reserved / total resources). On a shared cloud machine the last part is your vCPUs out of the host's vCPUs.
Few cloud providers publish embodied figures per instance, so most teams use a manufacturer's product footprint or a published estimate and label it as an assumption.

ul: It is not your company footprint. A company inventory reports total tonnes by scope; the SCI is a per-unit rate for one software system.

Offsets and renewable energy certificates cannot lower it. The specification excludes all market-based measures, so I must be the location-based intensity of the grid you draw from, and only cuts in energy, hardware or that grid intensity move the score.
It is not comparable across products unless the boundary and functional unit match. Publish both alongside the score.

p: Pick the unit your product scales with and that a customer understands. An API business uses calls, a collaboration tool uses active users, a data pipeline uses GB processed. Keep the same unit over time so the trend means something.

example.title: Worked example: one month of an API service in India
lines: Energy: one dedicated server averaging 1 kW for 720 hours = 720 kWh
Operational: 720 x 0.710 kg CO2 per kWh (CEA, version 21.0) = 511.2 kg
Embodied: assumed 1,500 kg CO2e for the server over a 4 year life (35,040 hours); 1,500 x 720 / 35,040 = 30.8 kg
example.note: The embodied figure is an illustrative assumption. The grid factor covers CO2 only; say so if you report the score as CO2e.

senseible: Senseible's cloud and data centre calculator turns vCPU-hours, memory, storage and network transfer into kWh and emissions by hosting region, which gives the E x I part. For servers on your own premises, it reads the kWh from your electricity bill and applies 0.710 kg CO2 per kWh.
